clause_svo.what: Who does what to whom: subject-verb-object candidates and clause tags, straight from the dependency parse.
clause_svo.how: Every parsed clause is tagged, and its subject, verb and object are pulled out as triples with their counts. The results are tables of the most frequent triples and clause types per document.
clause_svo.formula: No statistics here, just extraction: a verb with a nominal subject (nsubj) and object (dobj or obj) becomes one (subject, verb, object) triple, lemmatized, then counted. Passive constructions are labelled so the receiver can be told apart from the agent.
clause_svo.question: Does a collection of speeches talk about people doing things, or about things happening? Rank the triples and read who sits in the subject slot.
clause_svo.interpretation: Frequent triples are the corpus's stock phrasings, not proof of anyone's beliefs. Compare triple rates per 1,000 words between groups before calling a phrasing characteristic.
clause_svo.limits: Only clauses the parser recognises become triples; coordination and ellipsis are missed often. Pronoun subjects stay pronouns unless coreference is run first, so 'he signed' and 'Lincoln signed' are different triples.
clause_svo.settings: This tool has no settings of its own. Parse quality decides everything here, so if the triples look odd, inspect the parse on a passage first (the Interactive page shows it).
clause_svo.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
result = nlp.run("clause_svo", corpus)
nlp.show(result.table, title="Most frequent clause patterns")

collocations.what: Which words keep company: pairs that occur together more often than chance would predict.
collocations.how: Pairs are counted across sentences (adjacent words, or within a window), then scored by four association measures, so you can see whether a pairing survives only under one of them.
collocations.formula: With O the observed pair count and E the count expected if the words were independent: PMI = log2(O/E); PPMI is PMI clamped at zero; t-score = (O-E)/sqrt(O); z-score = (O-E)/sqrt(E). PMI flatters rare pairs, t-score favours frequent ones - agreement between them is the interesting signal.
collocations.question: What words cling to 'border' or 'economy' in this collection? Look for pairs strong by both PMI and t-score.
collocations.interpretation: A high PMI on a pair seen three times is usually noise; check the raw count column first. Collocates describe usage in this corpus only - a different collection will have different company.
collocations.limits: Function words and punctuation can dominate unless min-length and stopword choices filter them. Window counting admits pairs that never stand next to each other; adjacent counting misses flexible phrasings.
collocations.settings: field picks lemmas (groups inflections) or forms (keeps them apart). span=adjacent looks at neighbours only; span=window with window=5 looks at five words each side. min-count drops pairs seen less often (raise it to quiet rare noise), min-length drops short tokens, top-n keeps the strongest N rows. case-sensitive distinguishes 'March' from 'march'.
collocations.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
pairs = nlp.run("collocations", corpus, span="window", window=5, min_count=3).table
nlp.show(pairs, x="Collocate", y="PMI", kind="bar", title="Strongest collocates")

conll_wordlist.what: Ranked word lists by part of speech: the most frequent nouns, verbs, adjectives or adverbs in the corpus.
conll_wordlist.how: Tokens from the parse are grouped by their POS tag and counted, so the lists are grammar-aware rather than just raw frequency.
conll_wordlist.formula: Counts of each form or lemma within a POS category, ranked; no weighting or smoothing. Choose lemma to merge 'policy/policies' into one row, form to keep them apart.
conll_wordlist.question: Which nouns dominate this collection of editorials - and which verbs? Two ranked lists answer that in a minute.
conll_wordlist.interpretation: A top noun is frequent, not necessarily important; compare against another corpus with keyness before claiming it is characteristic. Rates beat counts when documents differ in length.
conll_wordlist.limits: POS tagging errors (especially on names and archaic spellings) leak into the lists. Category boundaries are the tagset's: 'all' mixes every class, and noun-verb is for words tagged either way.
conll_wordlist.settings: field: lemma or form. category limits the list to one part of speech (all, noun, verb, adjective, adverb, function, noun-verb). top-n keeps the first N. case-sensitive treats 'March' and 'march' as different words.
conll_wordlist.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
nouns = nlp.run("conll_wordlist", corpus, category="noun", top_n=25).table
nlp.show(nouns, x="Word", y="Count", kind="bar", title="Most frequent nouns")

corpus_statistics.what: The size and shape of each document: token counts, type counts, sentence counts and average lengths.
corpus_statistics.how: Computed per document from the parse (or raw text), then joinable by year or any document column so a corpus's growth or shrinkage over time is visible.
corpus_statistics.formula: Plain counts and means per document: tokens, unique types, sentences, mean sentence length (tokens/sentences) and mean word length (characters/token). TTR (types/tokens) is included but see lexical diversity's limits before reading it.
corpus_statistics.question: Do speeches get longer across periods? Plot Words and mean sentence length by Year and read the trend with your eyes first.
corpus_statistics.interpretation: Absolute counts mostly measure document length; use per-1,000-word rates when comparing. A rising mean sentence length is a syntactic fact about these documents, not a difficulty score.
corpus_statistics.limits: Tokenisation and sentence-splitting conventions set the numbers; another tool's counts may differ slightly. Very short documents make ratios wobble.
corpus_statistics.settings: field chooses what counts as a word unit: form (surface tokens) or lemma (dictionary forms merged). Everything else in the run form is about grouping and plotting, not counting.
corpus_statistics.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
stats = nlp.measures(corpus, which=["corpus_statistics"])
nlp.show(stats, x="Year", y="Words", kind="scatter", title="Document lengths over time")

dispersion.what: Whether a word is spread evenly through the corpus or bunched into a few documents - frequency alone cannot tell you.
dispersion.how: Each word's occurrences are split across parts (whole documents, or equal chunks), and its evenness of spread is scored. High frequency plus high concentration is a different finding from high frequency everywhere.
dispersion.formula: Gries' DP = half the sum of |f_i/N - 1/k| over k parts, where f_i is the count in part i and N the total: 0 means perfectly even, near 1 means one part holds everything. DPnorm divides DP by its maximum for this corpus's k, so corpora with different part counts can be compared. Juilland-style evenness is also reported; it runs in the opposite direction (high = even).
dispersion.question: Is 'freedom' a theme of the whole collection or of a few speeches? Cross frequency against DPnorm and look for frequent-but-concentrated words.
dispersion.interpretation: Low DP (or high evenness) with high frequency = a general theme. High DP with high frequency = a burst tied to specific documents - read those documents.
dispersion.limits: Part granularity decides the score: the same word can look dispersed by document and bursty by chunk. Words near min-count have unstable scores; short documents make document-level parts coarse.
dispersion.settings: field: lemma or form. parts=document (default) or chunk with chunks=N (equal slices of each document). min-count and min-length filter rare words and short tokens before ranking; top-n keeps the N most frequent candidates. plot draws frequency against concentration.
dispersion.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
spread = nlp.run("dispersion", corpus, parts="chunk", chunks=10, min_count=5).table
nlp.show(spread, x="Frequency", y="DP norm", kind="scatter", title="Frequency vs concentration")

doc_duplicates.what: Near-duplicate documents in the corpus - the same text filed twice under different names, lightly edited reprints and the like.
doc_duplicates.how: Every pair of documents is compared and the pairs above the similarity threshold are listed, so you can decide whether to drop one before it double-counts in every later analysis.
doc_duplicates.formula: Each document becomes a TF-IDF vector over its words; each pair is scored as cosine similarity (the same measure as document similarity) and pairs at or above threshold (default 80, on a 0-100 scale) are reported.
doc_duplicates.question: Before trusting any count: are any of these speeches copies of each other? Run this first on any corpus you did not type yourself.
doc_duplicates.interpretation: A pair at 95+ is almost certainly one text; 80-90 may be boilerplate shared by many documents (oaths, formulas). Inspect a couple of flagged pairs before deleting anything.
doc_duplicates.limits: Heavy paraphrase and translation evade TF-IDF overlap. Boilerplate inflates similarity for unrelated documents - lower it only if the false negatives matter more than the false alarms.
doc_duplicates.settings: threshold is the similarity score (0-100) at which a pair counts as a duplicate; 80 is the default. Raise it for fewer, clearer reports; lower it to catch lightly edited reprints at the cost of more pairs to read.
doc_duplicates.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
pairs = nlp.run("doc_duplicates", corpus, threshold=80).table
nlp.show(pairs, title="Documents that look like each other")

doc_similarity.what: Which documents resemble which: a matrix or neighbour list of pairwise similarity across the corpus.
doc_similarity.how: Documents are compared by their words (TF-IDF cosine), giving both a full matrix for the heat map and each document's closest matches.
doc_similarity.formula: Each document is a TF-IDF vector (tf x idf with the smoothed idf definition, same as the TF-IDF tool); similarity is the cosine of the two vectors, reported 0-100. stopwords can be removed before vectorising.
doc_similarity.question: Which speeches talk about the same things as this one? Use the neighbours table to find the matches, then read them side by side.
doc_similarity.interpretation: High similarity means shared vocabulary weighted by rarity - a thematic kinship, not agreement. The matrix's structure (blocks of similar documents) is often more informative than any single cell.
doc_similarity.limits: Shared boilerplate inflates similarity; synonymy defeats it (two documents about 'jobs' and 'employment' can score low). Short documents give unstable vectors.
doc_similarity.settings: threshold is the score (0-100) above which a pair is reported as neighbours; 80 is the default. stopwords: leave empty to keep every word, or name a built-in list to drop function words before comparing - often the difference between topical and syntactic similarity.
doc_similarity.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
matrix = nlp.run("doc_similarity", corpus, threshold=80).table
nlp.show(matrix, kind="heatmap", title="Document similarity")

k_sentences.what: The first and last sentences of every document, side by side - openings and closings as a reading corpus of their own.
k_sentences.how: Extracts k-first and k-last sentences per document into one table with document names and positions, ready to skim or feed to another tool.
k_sentences.formula: Sentence splitting on the parse; the first k and last k sentences of each document are copied out verbatim. No scoring, no selection heuristics.
k_sentences.question: How do these sermons open - with scripture, with a story, with a claim? Read thirty openings in one table and the pattern surfaces fast.
k_sentences.interpretation: These are complete sentences with names attached, so counts and rates over this table are counts over openings/closings only - label them that way in any write-up.
k_sentences.limits: Sentence segmentation errors show up immediately in extracted text. Documents shorter than k sentences are simply all opening and all closing; the table does not warn about it.
k_sentences.settings: k-first: how many sentences from the start of each document (default 2). k-last: how many from the end (default 2). Raise them for a wider window; lower to 1 for a clean 'opening sentence' corpus.
k_sentences.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
edges = nlp.run("k_sentences", corpus, k_first=1, k_last=1).table
nlp.show(edges, title="Openings and closings")

keyness.what: What words set one group of documents apart from another - the distinctive vocabulary of a period, party or author.
keyness.how: Two groups (chosen by any document column, or by a name pattern) are counted word by word and compared; the ranked output combines a significance measure with effect-size columns so a word can be statistically strong but trivially small.
keyness.formula: G2 log-likelihood: G2 = 2 * sum(O * ln(O/E)) over the four cells of a word's 2x2 table, with a 0.5 smoothing (Haldane-Anscombe) so zeros do not break the logarithm; the p-value comes from the chi-square distribution with 1 degree of freedom. Log Ratio = log2(rateA/rateB) is the effect size; Pct Diff and BIC are reported beside it.
keyness.question: What does a wartime legislature say that a peacetime one does not? Point the two groups at the periods and read the over-used column first.
keyness.interpretation: G2 says the difference is unlikely to be chance; Log Ratio says how big it is. Trust words with both a small p and a large log ratio, then check the raw counts so one document is not driving it.
keyness.limits: Documents differ in length, so rates decide the comparison - a long document can dominate pooled counts. Keyness is difference, not importance, and it is silent about words used equally in both groups. Multiple comparisons over thousands of words guarantee some small p-values by luck.
keyness.settings: group-field: the document column that defines the groups (e.g. Year or Party); group-a and group-b: the two values to compare, or group-pattern with a regular expression (used as group-a against 'everything else'). field: lemma or form. smoothing is added to every cell (0.5 by default; keep it positive). top-n keeps N words per direction.
keyness.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

early = nlp.corpus({"Year": range(1900, 1950)})
late = nlp.corpus({"Year": range(1950, 2000)})
keys = nlp.keyness(late, early, top_n=50)
nlp.show(keys, x="Word", y="Log Ratio", kind="bar", title="Words more typical of the later group")

kwic.what: Keyword in context: every occurrence of a word or pattern with the words around it, the classic concordance view.
kwic.how: Matches are pulled from the parsed text with a window of surrounding tokens and their document and position, so you can read how a word is actually used rather than only how often.
kwic.formula: Search over token forms or lemmas (or a regular expression over forms); each hit is one row with the left context, the match and the right context of `window` tokens. No scoring - it is a retrieval tool.
kwic.question: Is 'liberty' used about the nation or about the person? Read fifty contexts and you will know - that is the whole method.
kwic.interpretation: Clusters of use (all about 'economic', all in one period) are the finding; single rows are illustrations. Hit positions let you see whether uses gather at openings or endings.
kwic.limits: A fixed window can cut phrases in half; regex over forms misses lemma siblings unless you write them in. Max-hits silently truncates very common words - read the hit count before quoting proportions.
kwic.settings: query: the word, phrase or pattern to find. field: form or lemma matching. window: tokens of context each side (default 5). max-hits: stop after N matches (default 1000). case-sensitive: distinguish 'March' from 'march'. regex: treat query as a regular expression.
kwic.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
hits = nlp.run("kwic", corpus, query="border", field="lemma", window=5).table
nlp.show(hits, title="Every use of 'border' in context")

lexical_diversity.what: How varied a document's vocabulary is, measured four ways so the answer does not depend on one formula.
lexical_diversity.how: Each document is tokenised and scored with Guiraud, TTR, MTLD and vocd-D. All are length-sensitive in their own way, so compare like with like and read the length-check panel beside the scores.
lexical_diversity.formula: TTR = types/tokens. Guiraud = types/sqrt(tokens). MTLD (McCarthy & Jarvis) walks the token stream measuring how much of a 1.0 TTR-to-0.74 TTR drop each token explains, forward and backward, and averages the two (10-token floor). vocd-D fits D in the equation TTR = D/N^(0.5) by sampling token runs of 35-50 words 100 times (seeded) and keeping the mean best fit.
lexical_diversity.question: Do later essays reuse a smaller vocabulary than earlier ones? Compare MTLD across periods at similar document lengths.
lexical_diversity.interpretation: Higher scores mean more varied vocabulary at that length. MTLD and vocd-D survive length differences better than TTR and Guiraud; where they disagree, length or bursts of repetition is usually why.
lexical_diversity.limits: Every score falls as documents get longer; TTR fastest of all. Repetition of names and formulaic phrases lowers the score for structural reasons. Short texts give noisy MTLD/vocd-D - the length-check panel exists for this.
lexical_diversity.settings: seed fixes vocd-D's random sampling so two runs agree; change it only to test stability. No other settings: the four measures are always all reported.
lexical_diversity.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
diversity = nlp.measures(corpus, which=["lexical_diversity"])
nlp.show(diversity, x="Year", y="MTLD", kind="scatter", title="Vocabulary variety over time")

narrative.what: How a story moves: sentiment across the text, where characters appear, and who is named when.
narrative.how: Each document (or chapter) is cut into equal segments; tone and character mentions are charted against position, turning a whole book or speech collection into one readable curve.
narrative.formula: The emotion arc is VADER compound sentiment per segment, z-scored within the document so its shape is comparable across lengths. Character positions are each mention's location as a fraction through the text (0-1); the character-by-order heat strip aggregates those fractions into columns per document and rows per name.
narrative.question: Where do these memoirs turn dark - at the midpoint or near the end? Read the arc, then open the segments it dips over.
narrative.interpretation: The curve is a map of tone, not plot: a flat arc with a late dip is a finding about sentiment, which you then check against the text. Character density is about mentions, not importance.
narrative.limits: Segment count sets the resolution and the arc smooths local events away. Names miss nicknames and pronouns unless coreference or the gender tools have been run. Irony and negation still fool VADER in places.
narrative.settings: field: form (surface words) or lemma for the word-level work under the arc. Segmenting is fixed at equal fractions of each document so that different lengths line up.
narrative.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
result = nlp.run("narrative", corpus)
nlp.show(result.table, x="Position", y="Sentiment", kind="line", title="Emotion arc")

ner.what: Named people, places and organisations: who and what is mentioned, in which document, and where in it.
ner.how: A language model labels entity mentions in the parsed text; the results are a per-document entity timeline and a location-tracking table for place names.
ner.formula: Model-based sequence labelling (spaCy's English NER): each token span gets a label (PERSON, GPE, ORG, ...). Counts and rates are then grouped per entity per document; positions are fractions through the text.
ner.question: Which places do these travelogues actually name, and do the people mentioned change after 1900? The timeline answers both.
ner.interpretation: Mention counts are mentions, not significance - one speech naming a person twenty times still names one person. Compare rates per 1,000 words across groups of documents, and read a few contexts before quoting a name.
ner.limits: Models miss fictional, historical or non-English names and mislabel org/person borders; same-named people are merged. Common nouns can slip in as 'people' (the ignore list below filters the worst of these).
ner.settings: ignore: a comma-separated list of words never to report as entities - names that are also everyday words (e.g. 'Bill', 'Rose') or model noise. Everything else is fixed: the model is the installed English one.
ner.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
people = nlp.entities(corpus)
nlp.show(people, x="Entity", y="Count", kind="bar", title="Most mentioned entities")

ngram_cooccurrence.what: Which words share a neighbourhood: pairs that occur near each other within a moving window, with association scores and a network view.
ngram_cooccurrence.how: Within each sentence, words in a window of N tokens are counted as pairs; the strongest associations become a network where words are nodes and pair strength is the edge.
ngram_cooccurrence.formula: Co-occurrence counts O within the window, with expected count E from the words' independent rates; pairs are scored like collocations (PMI = log2(O/E) and companions), over lemmas or forms with min-count filtering.
ngram_cooccurrence.question: What vocabulary travels together in these sermons - which words are never far from 'sin' or 'grace'?
ngram_cooccurrence.interpretation: Dense clusters are semantic fields in this corpus; bridges between clusters are words used in two registers. Rare pairs need the count column read first, as with collocations.
ngram_cooccurrence.limits: Window size defines 'near': wide windows blur syntax into topic. A network layout is one of many equally good ones - trust the scores, not the picture's geometry.
ngram_cooccurrence.settings: window: how many tokens each side count as 'near' (default 5). field: lemma or form. min-count: drop pairs seen fewer times (default 1; raise it for cleaner networks).
ngram_cooccurrence.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
net = nlp.run("ngram_cooccurrence", corpus, window=5, min_count=2).table
nlp.show(net, title="Word neighbourhoods")

ngrams.what: Frequent word sequences of length n: bigrams, trigrams and beyond, with the collocation statistics for each.
ngrams.how: Every run of n consecutive tokens is counted, filtered by frequency and length, and ranked; collocation scores (PMI and companions) are attached to each phrase.
ngrams.formula: Counts of n consecutive tokens (forms or lemmas). Association columns follow the collocations measures: PMI = log2(O/E), t-score = (O-E)/sqrt(O), over the phrase's observed vs expected count.
ngrams.question: What phrases recur in these pamphlets - 'public good', 'free trade'? Start at n=2 and read the top fifty.
ngrams.interpretation: Frequency says what is said often; PMI says what is said characteristically. Multi-word terms are matched as phrases later by term_rates and search, so noting the exact wording here helps.
ngrams.limits: Tokenisation decides what an n-gram is (contractions, hyphens). The count falls steeply as n grows; rare long n-grams are almost always unique strings rather than phrases.
ngrams.settings: n: phrase length in tokens (default 2). field: form or lemma. min-count: minimum occurrences to report (default 2).
ngrams.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
phrases = nlp.run("ngrams", corpus, n=2, field="lemma", min_count=3).table
nlp.show(phrases, x="N-gram", y="Count", kind="bar", title="Most frequent bigrams")

nominalization.what: Deverbal nominalizations - 'governance' from govern, 'movement' from move: the nouns that let actions be talked about as things.
nominalization.how: Nouns built from verbs by the classic suffixes are detected in the parse (optionally against a curated list) and counted per document.
nominalization.formula: Candidate nouns matched by suffix (-tion, -ment, -ness, -ance and kin) and, when check-ending is on, checked against known verb stems; the curated list adds irregular cases ('deed', 'use'). Counts are raw hits of those lemmas.
nominalization.question: Do policy documents bury more actions in nouns than speeches do? Compare nominalization rates per 1,000 words across groups.
nominalization.interpretation: A higher rate means more action-as-thing phrasing - abstract, compressed, typical of official prose. It says nothing about whether the writing is good.
nominalization.limits: Suffixes overreach ('nation' looks deverbal but is not) and underreach (irregulars need the curated list). Rates rise with topic and register, so compare like texts.
nominalization.settings: field: lemma (groups inflections) or form. check-ending: require a plausible verb stem too (fewer false alarms, a little slower). curated-list: your own CSV of extra deverbal nouns to include.
nominalization.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
nominals = nlp.run("nominalization", corpus, check_ending=True).table
nlp.show(nominals, x="Document", y="Rate per 1000", kind="bar", title="Nominalization rate")

readability.what: Reading difficulty estimated from sentence length and syllable counts. Six formulas are reported side by side (Flesch Reading Ease, Flesch-Kincaid grade, Gunning Fog, Coleman-Liau, ARI and SMOG) rather than one magic number.
readability.how: Runs on each document's raw text - no parser, no model. Each formula gets its own column, because the scales differ and their agreement is itself evidence.
readability.formula: Flesch Reading Ease = 206.835 - 1.015 x (words/sentences) - 84.6 x (syllables/words). Flesch-Kincaid grade = 0.39 x (words/sentences) + 11.8 x (syllables/words) - 15.59. Gunning Fog = 0.4 x ((words/sentences) + 100 x (3+-syllable words/words)). Coleman-Liau = 0.0588 x L - 0.296 x S - 15.8, with L and S per 100 words. ARI = 4.71 x (characters/words) + 0.5 x (words/sentences) - 21.43. SMOG = 1.043 x sqrt(polysyllables x 30/sentences) + 3.1291 (needs 3+ sentences). Syllables come from the suite's heuristic counter, which is approximate.
readability.question: Did these speeches become easier to read across periods? Compare one column (say Flesch-Kincaid) across documents of similar length, then check a few passages yourself.
readability.interpretation: Higher Flesch Reading Ease means easier text; the grade-level scores run the other way (higher = harder). Read one formula across documents - mixing scales in one chart misleads. They are estimates of text surface, not of any real reader's experience.
readability.limits: Scores ignore argument quality, vocabulary rarity and an actual reader's understanding. Short passages, headings, abbreviations and OCR or transcription errors distort sentence and syllable counts badly; SMOG returns 0 for texts under three sentences.
readability.settings: This tool has no settings of its own - every document gets all six scores. Watch the inputs instead: texts under a few sentences should be excluded or read as unreliable.
readability.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
scores = nlp.measures(corpus, which=["readability"])
nlp.show(scores, x="Year", y="Flesch-Kincaid Grade", kind="scatter", title="Reading grade over time")

search.what: Find words or phrases anywhere in your documents - or in the parsed tokens and document columns - with plain or pattern matching.
search.how: One query runs over raw text (or CSV/CoNLL views) and returns hits with their documents, so you can jump from 'where is this word' to the passage itself.
search.formula: Retrieval, not statistics: exact substring matching (optionally case-sensitive) or a Python regular expression over the text, one row per hit with location and context.
search.question: Where does 'crisis' appear at all - and is it always in the same document? Run the search before theorising about it.
search.interpretation: Hit counts are occurrences; documents with any hits are a different and often more useful number. Read the contexts - the tool finds strings, not meanings.
search.limits: Exact matching misses inflections ('crisis' vs 'crises'); regex finds patterns like '1[89][0-9]{2}' but not ideas. This is not keyness: it cannot say a word is unusually frequent anywhere.
search.settings: query: the text or pattern to find. mode: search the raw text, a CSV or a CoNLL table. case-sensitive: distinguish 'March' from 'march'. regex: treat query as a regular expression.
search.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
hits = nlp.run("search", corpus, query="border", case_sensitive=False).table
nlp.show(hits, title="Every mention of 'border'")

sentence_complexity.what: How intricate the syntax is: how far words sit from their heads, how deep the trees go, how much subordination there is.
sentence_complexity.how: Measured per document from the dependency parse, one row of sentence-level syntax per document, joinable by year or author like every other measure.
sentence_complexity.formula: Mean dependency distance = mean |token id - head id| over headed words. Depth = the longest chain of head-links from a token up to the root. Subordination = subordinate-clause markers (advcl, ccomp, xcomp and kin) counted per sentence. All three need a parse, so this is among the slower tools.
sentence_complexity.question: Do speeches written for a second term use longer syntactic arms than first-term ones? Compare mean dependency distance at similar sentence lengths.
sentence_complexity.interpretation: Higher distance and depth mean more layered sentences - harder to parse for readers and machines alike. Subordination per sentence is often the most stable of the three across document lengths.
sentence_complexity.limits: Parse errors land here directly; coordinated and elliptical clauses distort distance. Translationese and poetic inversion produce high distances for readability the scores do not see. Compare within one language and register.
sentence_complexity.settings: This tool has no settings of its own; it always reports distance, depth and subordination. It does require the English parser (see Models).
sentence_complexity.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
syntax = nlp.measures(corpus, which=["sentence_complexity"])
nlp.show(syntax, x="Year", y="Mean Dependency Distance", kind="scatter", title="Syntactic complexity over time")

sentiment_vader_anew.what: Positive and negative tone in sentences and documents. VADER (a word-list method, always available) measures valence; optionally ANEW rates text on psychological dimensions from your own lexicon file.
sentiment_vader_anew.how: Runs on the parsed text, one row per sentence or document. VADER ships with the suite; ANEW is only run when you provide its ratings CSV.
sentiment_vader_anew.formula: VADER sums valence ratings for its lexicon words with rules for negation, degree modifiers ('very'), punctuation and capitalisation, then normalises to compound in [-1, 1] plus positive/neutral/negative proportions. ANEW averages each matched lemma's valence, arousal and dominance ratings from the lexicon you supply.
sentiment_vader_anew.question: Does tone swing across a campaign's speeches? Chart the compound score by date and read the sentences at each peak.
sentiment_vader_anew.interpretation: Compound near 0 is neutral; +1 and -1 are the extremes. Compare scores within one method - VADER and ANEW answer different questions. A document-level score hides mixed sentences, so open the sentence view before concluding.
sentiment_vader_anew.limits: Word lists misread sarcasm, domain jargon ('unemployment' is negative in VADER regardless of context) and long negation scopes. ANEW's ratings come from its original raters and era; scores are averages over matched words only.
sentiment_vader_anew.settings: analysis: vader only, or both (VADER plus ANEW). anew-lexicon: your ANEW ratings CSV when analysis=both. The desktop keeps only these two settings; scripts can also choose the matching field (form or lemma).
sentiment_vader_anew.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
tone = nlp.sentiment(corpus, model="vader", unit="document")
nlp.show(tone, x="Year", y="Compound", kind="line", title="Tone over time")

shapes.what: Story shape: the classic arcs of narrative - rise, fall, steady - drawn from the whole text, plus a Sankey view of how categories flow across sections.
shapes.how: The text is divided into equal segments and a key feature is charted across them (the story-arc panel), or named categories are flowed from section to section (the Sankey).
shapes.formula: Story arc: the text is split into equal-sized bins and each bin's prominence score (distinctive-term density or sentiment, standardised) is plotted in sequence - the TextArc/Gauss-Piper family of shapes. The shape_hc/shape_svd/shape_nmf tools below do the formal version: per-feature z-scores first, then clustering or decomposition.
shapes.question: Does this novella rise toward the middle or end? Run the arc on one text and name the shape before looking at another.
shapes.interpretation: Shapes are impressions of the whole - good for comparing several works in one glance, never for locating a scene. When comparing works, same bins and same feature are required or the shapes are not the same measurement.
shapes.limits: Resolution is the bin count; short texts give blocky arcs. The shape says nothing about genre expectations, irony or who speaks - it is one line through a complex object.
shapes.settings: sankey-source, sankey-target, sankey-value: column names for the Sankey view (leave empty for the story-arc panel). Everything else is fixed.
shapes.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
arc = nlp.run("shapes", corpus).table
nlp.show(arc, x="Position", y="Score", kind="line", title="Story shape")

spellcheck.what: Unfamiliar words in your documents, with spelling suggestions from a wordlist you choose. Your documents stay unchanged - this is a report, not a corrector (unless you ask).
spellcheck.how: Every word is checked against the wordlist; the unknown ones are listed with their counts and contexts, and their closest known spellings.
spellcheck.formula: Membership in the chosen wordlist decides 'unknown'. Suggestions are nearest neighbours by edit-distance similarity, reported when the similarity reaches threshold (default 80 on a 0-100 scale). OCR noise and archaic spellings therefore show up as unknown clusters.
spellcheck.question: How much of this manuscript is OCR noise? Sort the unknowns by count and look at the top - a scan problem announces itself.
spellcheck.interpretation: Names, archaic forms and technical terms are unknown by design; the interesting signal is dense clusters of near-words ('Govemment', 'Govemor') = systematic scan errors. Suggestions are candidates - read before accepting any correction.
spellcheck.limits: The wordlist is the measuring stick: a small list flags normal words. Edit distance mangles names into misleading suggestions. Nothing is written back unless the correction option is deliberately used.
spellcheck.settings: wordlist: your dictionary CSV (one column of known words). threshold: similarity (0-100) a suggestion must reach (default 80). correct: off by default - turn it on only to write suggested replacements back into the working copy (the originals are never touched).
spellcheck.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
unknowns = nlp.run("spellcheck", corpus, wordlist="my-dictionary.csv", threshold=80).table
nlp.show(unknowns, x="Word", y="Count", kind="bar", title="Most frequent unknown words")

style.what: Abstract or concrete? Familiar or strange? Rates documents on concreteness and iconicity from published word ratings.
style.how: Each lemma (or form) is matched to a ratings lexicon; document scores are the averages over matched words, with quality filters that drop unreliable ratings.
style.formula: Mean concreteness (or iconicity) rating over the document's matched types, weighted by frequency; unmatched words are skipped and the matched-word count is reported so coverage is visible. min-rating and max-rating-sd drop words whose raters disagreed or rated only extreme values.
style.question: Do these poems lean on concrete nouns more than the essays do? Compare mean concreteness with the matched-word counts in view.
style.interpretation: Higher concreteness = more imageable vocabulary; higher iconicity = more sound-symbolic words. Coverage (how many words matched) decides how much to trust any one document's score.
style.limits: Ratings come from specific rater populations and mostly single words out of context ('bank' has one rating). Figurative language shifts real concreteness without moving the score. Low-coverage documents have noisy means.
style.settings: analysis: concreteness or iconicity. field: lemma or form. concreteness-lexicon / iconicity-lexicon: your ratings CSVs when not using the built-ins. min-rating (default 5.0): drop words whose mean rating is below this reliability floor; max-rating-sd (default 2.0): drop words raters disagreed about.
style.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
style = nlp.run("style", corpus, analysis="concreteness").table
nlp.show(style, x="Document", y="Mean Concreteness", kind="bar", title="Abstract vs concrete")

svo_compare.what: Two groups side by side as subject-verb-object triples: which doings belong to which collection.
svo_compare.how: Runs the same SVO extraction as clause_svo over two document groups, then contrasts the triples - shared ones, and the ones each group owns.
svo_compare.formula: Triples extracted from the parse (see clause_svo) and counted per group; contrast columns follow the keyness logic (G2 over the two count columns) and a cosine over triple vectors gives each triple's opposite in the other group.
svo_compare.question: Who acts in the novels and who acts in the speeches - literally, which subjects take which verbs?
svo_compare.interpretation: Group-specific triples are phrasing habits of that group at this size; shared triples are the common ground. Rates, not raw counts, compare groups fairly.
svo_compare.limits: All of clause_svo's extraction limits apply twice. Pronoun subjects stay pronouns, so 'he struck' and 'the king struck' are separate rows until coreference is run.
svo_compare.settings: This tool has no settings of its own: the two groups come from the run form's group choices (a document column and two values).
svo_compare.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

early = nlp.corpus({"Year": range(1900, 1950)})
late = nlp.corpus({"Year": range(1950, 2000)})
# For triple-level contrast, run clause_svo on each and compare its tables:
a = nlp.run("clause_svo", early).table
b = nlp.run("clause_svo", late).table
nlp.show(a, title="Clause patterns, early group")

table_charts.what: Publication-ready charts over any CSV of yours - bar, line, scatter, histogram, box, heatmap and more - with the rate and share calculations built in.
table_charts.how: Point it at an original data CSV (not corpus text), name the columns to plot and aggregate, and it draws the figure as HTML or PNG. This is for analyst spreadsheets; corpus results already carry their own charts.
table_charts.formula: Whatever aggregation you choose (sum, mean, median or count) over the y-column per x-category (or per group series). rate-per divides by a denominator column scaled per total, group or category; normalize turns values into percentages or shares. It is arithmetic you could write yourself, minus the mistakes.
table_charts.question: Got a spreadsheet of mentions by year and newspaper? This is a chart of it in thirty seconds, share-ready.
table_charts.interpretation: The chart shows the aggregation you picked - 'mean of counts' is often not what a reader assumes. Say the aggregation in the caption; the export keeps it in the settings.
table_charts.limits: CSV garbage in, chart garbage out: mixed types and empty cells choose odd aggregations. HTML format needs no browser install; the packaged export may offer fewer formats. This tool does not analyse corpus text at all.
table_charts.settings: input: your CSV. kind: bar, line, scatter, histogram, box, heatmap, pie and friends. x and y: the columns to plot; group: the series/colour column. agg: sum, mean, median or count. normalize: none, percent or share. rate-per with denominator-column: chart a rate instead of a raw count, scaled by total, group or category. top-n keeps the N biggest categories. bins: histogram bin count. title, x-label, y-label: what the reader sees. format: html, png, svg, pdf or xlsx. The rest (width, height, wrap-labels, x-tick-angle, delimiter, encoding) tune the layout and file reading.
table_charts.example:
import pandas as pd
import nlpsuite as nlp

data = pd.read_csv("mentions.csv")  # the CSV you would choose in the form
summary = data.groupby("Year")["Count"].sum().reset_index()
nlp.show(summary, x="Year", y="Count", kind="line", title="Mentions per year")
nlp.save(summary, "mentions_per_year")

table_chi2.what: Chi-square test of association between two categorical columns of a CSV - plus residuals, so you can see which cells make the result significant.
table_chi2.how: Builds the contingency table of your two columns, tests it, and reports chi-square, p, degrees of freedom and the standardised residuals that show where the association lives.
table_chi2.formula: chi2 = sum((O - E)^2 / E) over the cells of the contingency table, with E = row total x column total / N; p from the chi-square distribution with (rows-1)(cols-1) degrees of freedom. Standardised residuals are (O - E)/sqrt(E), the per-cell contribution; the significance level alpha (default 0.05) is what the report is judged against.
table_chi2.question: Is mentioning the economy actually associated with party, in your coding spreadsheet? The residuals name the cells to read up on.
table_chi2.interpretation: A small p says the columns are associated, not why or how strongly. Residuals above about |2| mark the cells driving it; a big table with tiny cell counts can be significant for boring reasons.
table_chi2.limits: Expected counts under 5 make the chi-square approximation unreliable (collapse rare categories first). Association is not causation, and a spreadsheet's coding choices are invisible to the test.
table_chi2.settings: input: the original data CSV. col1, col2: the exact column headings to test. alpha: significance level strictly between 0 and 1 (default 0.05) - move it only as your discipline demands, before looking at results.
table_chi2.example:
import pandas as pd
from scipy.stats import chi2_contingency
import nlpsuite as nlp

data = pd.read_csv("your-data.csv")  # the same CSV you would choose in the form
counts = pd.crosstab(data["Party"], data["Position"])
chi2, p, dof, expected = chi2_contingency(counts)
nlp.note(f"chi2({dof}) = {chi2:.2f}, p = {p:.4f}")
nlp.show(counts, kind="heatmap", title="Observed counts")

table_crosstab.what: Cross-tabulated counts and row percentages for two categorical columns - the contingency table behind every chi-square.
table_crosstab.how: Counts every combination of the two columns and shows counts and row percentages side by side, so the pattern can be read before any test is run.
table_crosstab.formula: Cell count = number of rows with that (col1, col2) combination; row percentage = cell / row total x 100. No smoothing, no test - just the table.
table_crosstab.question: How is your coded material distributed across category and period? Look at the percentages before deciding there is anything to test.
table_crosstab.interpretation: Row percentages answer 'within this row, how is it spread'; mind which margin the percentages use. Raw counts belong beside them so a 50% share of twelve items is not read as a finding.
table_crosstab.limits: Sparse tables produce dramatic percentages on thin evidence. The table only reflects the coding in your CSV; category order is the file's, not the meaning's.
table_crosstab.settings: input: the original data CSV. col1, col2: the exact column headings to cross. No other settings - the output is always counts plus row percentages.
table_crosstab.example:
import pandas as pd
import nlpsuite as nlp

data = pd.read_csv("your-data.csv")
table = pd.crosstab(data["Party"], data["Position"], normalize="index").round(3) * 100
nlp.show(table, kind="heatmap", title="Row percentages")

table_keyness.what: Keyword comparison between two frequency columns of a CSV: log-likelihood over counts you already have, without re-counting text.
table_keyness.how: Give it a word column and two count columns (two corpora, two periods, two authors); it ranks the words by how sharply each column differs from the other.
table_keyness.formula: G2 log-likelihood over each word's 2x2 table of (word/not-word) x (corpus1/corpus2): G2 = 2 * sum(O * ln(O/E)), p from chi-square with 1 df; the log ratio gives effect size. This is the same keyness mathematics as the corpus tool, applied to columns.
table_keyness.question: Comparing frequency lists from outside the suite? Which words does column 2 use disproportionately more - and by how much?
table_keyness.interpretation: Small p + large log ratio = the words worth reading contexts for. The columns' totals matter: rates are what G2 compares under the hood.
table_keyness.limits: Counts must be real counts of comparable things - two lists with different tokenisations make the test compare conventions. Rare words get large ratios from noise; use the count columns.
table_keyness.settings: input: the original CSV of frequency counts. word-col: the column naming each word. freq1, freq2: the two count columns to compare.
table_keyness.example:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import nlpsuite as nlp

counts = pd.read_csv("frequencies.csv")  # columns: word, before, after
rate1 = counts["before"] / counts["before"].sum()
rate2 = counts["after"] / counts["after"].sum()
counts["Log Ratio"] = np.log2((rate2 + 1e-9) / (rate1 + 1e-9))
top = counts.sort_values("Log Ratio", ascending=False).head(20)
nlp.show(top, x="word", y="Log Ratio", kind="bar", title="Words that grew")

table_kw.what: Kruskal-Wallis test over three or more groups in a CSV, with Dunn post-hoc comparisons saying which groups actually differ.
table_kw.how: Ranks the values across all groups, tests whether at least one group differs, then compares the groups in pairs with a multiple-comparison correction.
table_kw.formula: Kruskal-Wallis H = the rank-variance statistic over all groups (chi-square distributed with k-1 df) - the non-parametric cousin of one-way ANOVA. Dunn's pairwise tests compare mean ranks between two groups; Holm (default) or Bonferroni corrects the pile of pairwise p-values so the family-wise error stays near alpha (default 0.05).
table_kw.question: Do word counts differ across four periods at all - and between which periods exactly? The post-hoc table names the pairs.
table_kw.interpretation: A significant H only says 'somewhere there is a difference'; Dunn's rows say where. Report medians beside the p-values - the test works on ranks, and ranks are about order, not distance.
table_kw.limits: Groups need enough observations for ranks to mean anything; ties (common in small integer data) weaken the approximation. Non-parametric does not mean assumption-free: independent observations are still required.
table_kw.settings: input: the original data CSV. value-col: the numeric column measured. group-col: the column naming the groups. alpha: significance level strictly between 0 and 1 (default 0.05). posthoc-method: holm (default, recommended) or bonferroni (stricter).
table_kw.example:
import pandas as pd
from scipy.stats import kruskal
import nlpsuite as nlp

data = pd.read_csv("your-data.csv")
groups = [g["Count"].values for _, g in data.groupby("Period")]
stat, p = kruskal(*groups)
nlp.note(f"Kruskal-Wallis H = {stat:.2f}, p = {p:.4f}")
nlp.show(data.groupby("Period")["Count"].median().reset_index(), x="Period", y="Count", kind="bar", title="Median per period")

table_mw.what: Mann-Whitney comparison of two groups in a CSV: does one group's values sit higher than the other's, without assuming a normal distribution?
table_mw.how: Ranks both groups' values together and tests whether one group is systematically higher; reports the test statistic, p and both group medians.
table_mw.formula: Mann-Whitney U on the pooled ranks of the two groups (the non-parametric two-sample test); p from the normal approximation with tie correction, judged at alpha (default 0.05). Medians and counts are reported beside it because U works on order only.
table_mw.question: Are later letters longer than earlier ones in your spreadsheet? The medians and p answer it without any bell-curve hoping.
table_mw.interpretation: A small p says one group tends higher - which one the medians say. It is not a test of means; a significant result with near-equal medians usually means a shape difference in the tails.
table_mw.limits: Ties and very small groups blur the p-value; unequal spread across groups complicates the 'tends higher' reading. Two columns coded from different sources can differ for reasons the test cannot see.
table_mw.settings: input: the original data CSV. value-col: the numeric column measured. group-col: the column with exactly two group values. alpha: significance level strictly between 0 and 1 (default 0.05).
table_mw.example:
import pandas as pd
from scipy.stats import mannwhitneyu
import nlpsuite as nlp

data = pd.read_csv("your-data.csv")
a = data.loc[data["Period"] == "early", "Count"]
b = data.loc[data["Period"] == "late", "Count"]
stat, p = mannwhitneyu(a, b)
nlp.note(f"U = {stat:.0f}, p = {p:.4f}; medians {a.median():.0f} vs {b.median():.0f}")

table_rankcorr.what: Rank correlation between two numeric columns of a CSV: Spearman's rho or Kendall's tau, with the p-value.
table_rankcorr.how: Ranks both columns and measures their agreement - the test to use when the relationship is monotonic but not linear, or the columns are ordinal scores.
table_rankcorr.formula: Spearman rho = Pearson correlation of the ranks; Kendall tau = (concordant pairs - discordant pairs) / total pairs. Both run 1 (perfect agreement in order) through 0 to -1 (perfect reversal); p tests rho/tau = 0.
table_rankcorr.question: Does a document's readability score track its year in your export? Rho answers it even if the relationship is a curve rather than a line.
table_rankcorr.interpretation: Rho/tau near +/-1 means the two columns order the rows almost identically. Tau is the better-behaved choice for small samples and many ties; rho magnitudes read larger by construction, so do not compare them directly.
table_rankcorr.limits: Monotonic only: a U-shaped relationship gives rho near 0 despite a perfect pattern. Ties deflate both measures. Correlation of two columns is not evidence that one causes the other.
table_rankcorr.settings: input: the original data CSV. col-x, col-y: the two numeric columns. method: spearman (default) or kendall.
table_rankcorr.example:
import pandas as pd
from scipy.stats import spearmanr
import nlpsuite as nlp

data = pd.read_csv("your-data.csv")
rho, p = spearmanr(data["Year"], data["Words"])
nlp.note(f"Spearman rho = {rho:.3f}, p = {p:.4f}")

table_search.what: Find rows in a parsed token table by column conditions - the CoNLL equivalent of 'select rows where', with AND/OR logic.
table_search.how: Filters the parsed tokens of your corpus by one or more column tests (equals, contains, starts/ends with, regex), returning the matching rows and their context columns.
table_search.formula: Row-wise boolean tests over the chosen token columns, joined with AND or OR: each test is equality, substring, prefix, suffix or a Python regex. Negate flips the selection. No scoring - it is a filtered view of the parse.
table_search.question: Show me every noun tagged after a preposition in these documents - the filter is the analysis, the table is your evidence.
table_search.interpretation: The rows are your population for whatever follows (counts by hand, reading, a chart). Rates over filtered rows need the corpus's totals as denominator, which the run's other tables carry.
table_search.limits: Depends entirely on parse accuracy and the tagset's column values; a typo in value yields an empty table with no error. Regex over Form is surface-only.
table_search.settings: field: which token column to test (e.g. Form, Lemma, POS, DepRel - empty means all text columns). value: the value or pattern to look for. op: eq, contains, starts_with, ends_with or regex. logic: AND or OR across conditions. case-sensitive: distinguish case. negate: invert the selection.
table_search.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
rows = nlp.run("table_search", corpus, field="POS", value="NOUN", op="eq").table
nlp.show(rows, title="Every noun token")

table_trend.what: Mann-Kendall trend test and Sen's slope over dated observations in a CSV: is the series going up, down or nowhere?
table_trend.how: Works on ranks of consecutive observations - robust to outliers and to non-normal noise - and reports the direction, significance and the slope in units per observation.
table_trend.formula: Mann-Kendall S = (concordant - discordant pairs over time) with variance corrected for ties; the p-value tests S = 0 (no monotonic trend). Sen's slope = the median of all pairwise slopes (y_j - y_i)/(j - i) between observations, which is the trend's size in value-units per step.
table_trend.question: Is vocabulary diversity really declining across these decades in your exports? The slope says how much per observation.
table_trend.interpretation: Significant S says monotonic direction; Sen's slope says how steeply, in the value's own units per step. A flat slope with tiny p can happen with many observations - report both.
table_trend.limits: Serial correlation (year-to-year autocorrelation) inflates significance badly - smooth or block first for annual series. Monotonic trends only: rise-then-fall gives S near 0. Uneven date spacing treats steps as equal.
table_trend.settings: input: the original data CSV. date-col: the ordering column (dates or years). value-col: the measured column. The observations are sorted by date internally; duplicates in date are kept in file order.
table_trend.example:
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import nlpsuite as nlp

data = pd.read_csv("series.csv").sort_values("Year")
x = data["Year"].to_numpy()
y = data["Score"].to_numpy()
slopes = [(y[j] - y[i]) / (x[j] - x[i]) for i in range(len(x)) for j in range(i + 1, len(x))]
sen = float(np.median(slopes))
nlp.note(f"Sen slope = {sen:.3f} per year")
nlp.show(data, x="Year", y="Score", kind="line", title="The series")

table_wordcloud_gephi.what: Word clouds and Gephi-ready network files from any CSV: frequency clouds in one click, or an edge list for Gephi in the next.
table_wordcloud_gephi.how: Point it at a CSV with a word column and a weight column (or source/target columns for network mode); it draws the cloud or writes a .gexf graph file for Gephi.
table_wordcloud_gephi.formula: Word cloud: font size scales with the chosen weight (count or rate), down to max-words. Gexf mode: each row becomes an edge (source-col to target-col) with weight-col as its weight, written as GEXF XML - no statistics, a file format.
table_wordcloud_gephi.question: Have a frequency list from anywhere and want a figure in a minute - or a network to open in Gephi? Both modes are one form.
table_wordcloud_gephi.interpretation: Cloud sizes are the weights you supplied (garbage in, garbage out); the PNG/HTML is a figure, not evidence on its own. For Gexf, weights decide Gephi's layout as much as structure does.
table_wordcloud_gephi.limits: Clouds distort perception of differences (area is not linear in value) and are weak for close frequencies. Gexf needs source and target columns to be real node names; isolated nodes come from rows you did not include.
table_wordcloud_gephi.settings: input: the original CSV. mode: wordcloud or gexf. word-col and weight-col: for clouds; source-col, target-col for networks. max-words: cloud vocabulary size (default 100). image: also render a raster PNG. title: what the figure says. mask and shape: optional silhouette for the cloud; group-col and colors colour by category; colormap, background, width, height and seed tune the drawing (seed fixes the layout between runs).
table_wordcloud_gephi.example:
import pandas as pd
import nlpsuite as nlp

freq = pd.read_csv("frequencies.csv")  # columns: word, count
top = freq.nlargest(50, "count")
nlp.show(top, x="word", y="count", kind="bar", title="Top 50 words")
# The cloud itself comes from the table tool on the Analyze page; the
# notebook keeps the same numbers in a chart that reads more precisely.

text_statistics.what: The classic counts of linguistic form: word and sentence lengths, type-token ratios, POS mix, Yule's K and companions, per document.
text_statistics.how: Derived from the parsed token table, one row per document with a band of structural measures - the fast overview before any heavier tool.
text_statistics.formula: Means of sentence length (tokens per sentence) and word length (characters per token); TTR = types/tokens; Yule's K = 10^4 * (sum(i^2 * V_i) / N^2 - 1/N) over the frequency spectrum V_i (words seen i times) - higher K means more repetition. POS columns are counts per tag family; ratios over them describe sentence make-up.
text_statistics.question: Does the register shift between the letters and the sermons? Read the POS mix and Yule's K side by side before touching sentiment.
text_statistics.interpretation: This is a fingerprint of form, not meaning. Big moves in Yule's K mean repetition changed; POS shifts (more pronouns, fewer nouns) are the structural story of a corpus.
text_statistics.limits: Length-sensitive measures (TTR especially) punish long documents - see lexical diversity before comparing across lengths. Parse tagging errors land in the POS columns. Corpus conventions (word counting) make small differences across tools normal.
text_statistics.settings: field: form (surface tokens) or lemma (dictionary forms merged). Everything else is computed the same way every time.
text_statistics.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
stats = nlp.measures(corpus, which=["text_statistics"])
nlp.show(stats, x="Year", y="Yule's K", kind="scatter", title="Repetition over time")

tfidf.what: Which words are weighted as distinctive in each document - the classic term-frequency/inverse-document-frequency score behind search engines and document comparison.
tfidf.how: Every document's vocabulary is weighted: frequent in this document, rare across the corpus, tops the list. The output is a per-document ranking of its most characteristic terms.
tfidf.formula: weight = tf * idf. idf = ln((1 + N) / (1 + df)) + 1 (the smoothed 'sklearn' convention: a term in every document gets idf 1, not 0). tf is raw count by default; sublinear-tf replaces it with 1 + ln(tf). max-df-ratio (default 0.5) drops terms appearing in more than half the documents first - boilerplate words die here.
tfidf.question: What single word distinguishes this document from the rest of the collection? The top rows answer exactly that.
tfidf.interpretation: High-weight terms are distinctive here, not important overall - cross-read with keyness for the group question. The heat map of top terms across documents shows a collection's structure at a glance.
tfidf.limits: IDF is collection-relative: add documents and old weights move. One-word tokens only (no phrases - use ngrams first). Very short documents produce noisy tops; min-df and min-length are the guards.
tfidf.settings: field: lemma or form. top-n: terms kept per document (default 20). min-df / max-df-ratio: drop terms appearing in fewer than N documents / more than this share of documents (0.5 default). min-length: drop short tokens. sublinear-tf: log-scale the term counts (often better for long documents). no-normalize: keep raw tf * idf without the usual vector normalisation.
tfidf.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
weights = nlp.run("tfidf", corpus, top_n=10, min_df=2).table
nlp.show(weights, title="Most distinctive words per document")

lexicon_series.what: How often a word list you define appears over time (or by any grouping) - rates per 1,000 words, ready to chart.
lexicon_series.how: Name a word group (or several), pick the grouping (year, decade, document, order, or a pattern over names), and get a rate series plus a heat map of the groups.
lexicon_series.formula: Count of each group's words (lemma, form or exact-lowercase matching) per grouping unit, divided by that unit's words and scaled by `per` (default 1,000). Group totals sum the member words; within= restricts counting to matching documents.
lexicon_series.question: Does 'opportunity' rise while 'duty' falls? Define both groups and read the two lines on one chart.
lexicon_series.interpretation: Rates, not counts - always. A rising line means denser usage, not more speeches about it. Group sizes differ; the pooled-by-period line smooths what the per-document dots show honestly.
lexicon_series.limits: The word list is the theory: inflections must be listed for exact-lowercase; lemma matching needs the parser and a dictionary form. Sparse periods make jagged rates; order grouping needs ordered documents (books, chapters).
lexicon_series.settings: terms: your word groups ('Name: word, word; Other: word' or a lexicon CSV). by: year, decade, document, order, period or a group-pattern (a regex over document names). field: lemma or form (match='exact-lowercase' is available in scripts for hand-counted runs). within: only count in documents whose name matches this pattern. group-pattern: the regex defining custom groups.
lexicon_series.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
series = nlp.term_rates(
    corpus,
    {"duty": ["duty", "duties"], "opportunity": ["opportunity", "opportunities"]},
    per=1000,
    by="year",
    match="exact-lowercase",
)
nlp.show(series, x="Year", y=["duty per 1000", "opportunity per 1000"], kind="line", title="Two vocabularies over time")

lda_gensim.what: Topic model: k clusters of co-occurring words, each document's mix of them, built on the parsed text with gensim's LDA.
lda_gensim.how: The corpus is turned into a bag of lemmas (or forms), LDA fits k topics of weighted words, and the tables show each topic's terms, each document's dominant topic and the full mix.
lda_gensim.formula: Latent Dirichlet Allocation (Blei, Ng & Jordan 2003): each document is a mixture of topics, each topic a distribution over words, fitted by variational Bayes (gensim). The relevance column uses lambda (default 0.6) to rank terms: lambda * log p(term|topic) + (1-lambda) * log lift (Sievert & Shirley's relevance).
lda_gensim.question: What themes does this archive hold without me naming any? Ask for 5 topics and read the top words before trusting any label.
lda_gensim.interpretation: Topics are word-distribution patterns, not themes with names - label them only after reading their top terms and a document or two. Different seeds can give different models; lda_stability tests that.
lda_gensim.limits: Bag-of-words ignores syntax and negation; k is a guess you impose. Rare words and stopwords steer the fit (the options below control both). LDA finds what is lexically clustered, which need not be what a reader calls a theme.
lda_gensim.settings: field: lemma (default) or form. topics: how many to fit (default 3 - try several). top-n: words shown per topic. seed: fitting start (same seed = same result). nouns-only: restrict to nouns. keep-stopwords: keep function words (off by default). lambda: term-relevance trade-off (0.6 default; 1.0 = within-topic probability, 0.0 = distinctiveness).
lda_gensim.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
result = nlp.topics(corpus, k=5, seed=100)
print(result.tables)  # the tables the model produced
nlp.show(result.table, title="Topics")

lda_mallet.what: Topic model with MALLET's LDA - the classic Java implementation, on raw text rather than parsed tokens.
lda_mallet.how: Available on the Analyze page when the MALLET toolkit is installed beside the app; it trains on the documents and returns topics and document-topic mixtures like the gensim version.
lda_mallet.formula: LDA as implemented by MALLET (McCallum et al.), Gibbs-sampled rather than variational: the same document-mixture/word-distribution model as lda_gensim with a different optimiser, which often gives crisper topics on longer texts.
lda_mallet.question: Does MALLET's sampling separate these themes where gensim blurred them? Same corpus, same k, compare the top terms.
lda_mallet.interpretation: Read exactly as lda_gensim: labels come after the evidence. Gibbs sampling is stochastic across runs; the seed parameter exists so a run can be repeated.
lda_mallet.limits: Needs the separately installed MALLET toolkit - without it the run fails with a message rather than results. Not available in notebooks (no nlp.run name); the gensim model covers notebook use. Same bag-of-words limits as any LDA.
lda_mallet.settings: topics: how many to fit (default 10). seed: sampling start. Both live on the Analyze page form; there is no notebook entry point for this tool.
lda_mallet.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
# MALLET runs from the Analyze page (it needs the separate install).
# In a notebook the included LDA is the one to use:
result = nlp.topics(corpus, k=5, seed=100)
nlp.show(result.table, title="Topics (gensim LDA)")

gender_annotator.what: Which characters are named as female or male in the text, by first-name dictionaries - a character census, not a guess at the author.
gender_annotator.how: First names of entity mentions (or proper nouns) are matched against a name dictionary; per document you get counts and a mentions-over-time view of who is named.
gender_annotator.formula: Name lookup: a PERSON's first token is checked against the chosen dictionary (census, Carnegie Mellon, NLTK names, or social security data), which carries gender labels from its source. Counts are mentions per document; no probability, no inference from pronouns.
gender_annotator.question: Whose names does this collection actually name - and does it change across periods? The counts say who is mentioned, the timeline says when.
gender_annotator.interpretation: Mentions of names labelled in a dictionary, counted - that is all. The dictionaries' labels come from administrative data and get names like 'James' wrong across eras and cultures; treat the three-way split as approximate.
gender_annotator.limits: Initials, surnames used alone, nicknames and non-Western names are unmatched or mislabelled. The dictionary's gender labels are its authors' categories, not the text's; unknown names are simply absent from the counts.
gender_annotator.settings: dictionary: census, carnegie_mellon, nltk or social_security (each with its own coverage and era). names-dir: your own dictionary folder to use instead. source: ner (PERSON entities from the model) or propn (every proper noun). Field choices (form/lemma) apply to the name tokens.
gender_annotator.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
result = nlp.run("gender_annotator", corpus, dictionary="census", source="ner")
nlp.show(result.table, title="Whose names appear")

date_annotator.what: Dates and periods mentioned in the text, pulled out and placed on a timeline - when the documents say things happened.
date_annotator.how: Recognises explicit years, full dates and period names in raw text (no parser needed) and collects them per document with their kind and context.
date_annotator.formula: Pattern-based recognition of year and date forms within the min-year/max-year bounds (defaults 1000-2100), plus named periods. Bare numbers count as years only when a date word ('year', 'century', 'in') stands nearby or the number sits alone in a heading line - so '1500 soldiers' is a count, not a year. Every classification is recorded in the run's diagnostics.
date_annotator.question: Which decades do these letters actually talk about, whatever their own date? The timeline is the map of their historical attention.
date_annotator.interpretation: These are mentioned dates, not document dates - the timeline shows what the texts refer to. Counts of years are mentions; a single memoir can dominate them.
date_annotator.limits: Implicit and relative dates ('last Tuesday', 'a decade ago') are missed by design. Archival spellings and OCR errors break patterns. The bare-number rule is conservative: some real years without context will be skipped rather than guessed.
date_annotator.settings: min-year and max-year: the range of plausible years (1000-2100 by default) - narrow them if numbers like measurements keep landing near the edges. No parser required.
date_annotator.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
dates = nlp.run("date_annotator", corpus, min_year=1500, max_year=2000).table
nlp.show(dates, x="Year", y="Count", kind="bar", title="Years the texts mention")

quote_annotator.what: Reported speech and quotations, with their speakers: who is quoted, how much, and at what length.
quote_annotator.how: Quotation spans are detected in the parsed text and attributed to the nearest plausible speaker mention; results are a speakers table and quote rates per document.
quote_annotator.formula: Quote boundaries from quotation marks and reporting clauses in the parse; attribution attaches a quote to the nearest PERSON mention in the same sentence or the one before (a heuristic, flagged where ambiguous). Pronouns ('he said') are kept as (pronoun) rather than being guessed into a name.
quote_annotator.question: How much of this report is quotation rather than narration - and whose voices? The rate and speakers tables answer together.
quote_annotator.interpretation: Quote rate is the share of text inside quotation marks; speaker counts are attributions the heuristic managed. Reads of 'who speaks' need a pass over the quote contexts.
quote_annotator.limits: Single quotes, nested quotes and unmarked speech defeat the boundary detection. Attribution is nearest-mention and gets long dialogues wrong; (pronoun) rows are honest non-answers. Dramatic texts with turn-taking (no reporting verbs) attribute poorly.
quote_annotator.settings: min-length: the shortest span in characters to count as a quote (default 1). Everything else is the heuristic as described; attribution quality is a property of the text's style.
quote_annotator.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
result = nlp.run("quote_annotator", corpus, min_length=2)
nlp.show(result.table, title="Who is quoted")

gender_guess.what: Writing style features associated with author gender in the classic stylometric studies - formal features, informal ones, or both.
gender_guess.how: Counts the function-word and marker lists from the tradition (Rayson et al.'s log-likelihood studies of male/female correspondence) per document and rates them per 1000 words.
gender_guess.formula: Frequency rates of two marker sets: formal markers (articles, prepositions, long words and kin) and informal ones (pronouns, emotion words, hedges, abbreviations). The tool reports the rates; any comparison of groups is left to you (the lists' provenance is in the references of the original studies).
gender_guess.question: Do these letters use the hedging and pronoun markers of the informal set more than those memoirs? Compare rates - and read the studies' own caveats first.
gender_guess.interpretation: Higher rates mean denser use of those markers - period and genre move them as much as authorship does. A group difference is a difference in this corpus's style lists, not a test of anyone's gender.
gender_guess.limits: The gender framing is historical baggage of the source studies; the markers really measure register. Author gender is unknowable from these counts and is not inferred here. Genre and era confound every comparison.
gender_guess.settings: mode: formal (the formal marker set), informal (the informal set) or both (default). The lists are fixed; scripts get the same rates via nlp.run.
gender_guess.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
style = nlp.run("gender_guess", corpus, mode="both").table
nlp.show(style, x="Document", y="Rate per 1000", kind="bar", title="Marker densities")

verb_analysis.what: The verbs of the corpus in aggregate: tense mix, voice mix (active vs passive), and modality - the machinery of assertion.
verb_analysis.how: Every verb group in the parse is classified along three axes and counted per document, giving each document a profile of how it states things.
verb_analysis.formula: From the parse's morphological features and auxiliaries: tense from VerbForm/Tense tags (past, present, future via 'will/shall'), voice from passive auxiliaries + nsubj:pass, modality from modal auxiliaries (can, must, should...) grouped as possibility/necessity/knowledge. Counts per document, rates per 1,000 words in the panels.
verb_analysis.question: Does this legislation commit ('shall') more than it suggests ('may')? The modality mix is one chart answering it.
verb_analysis.interpretation: Passive density means receivers outnumber named agents in the syntax - a fact about presentation, not responsibility. Modal counts tell you how obligations are worded, not how binding they are.
verb_analysis.limits: Tagging errors land here; English 'be + -ed' ambiguity moves passive counts. Modal uses with ellipsis or idiom are misgrouped. Cross-language comparison is out of scope for the English parse.
verb_analysis.settings: analysis: all (default), modality, tense or voice - pick one axis to run alone. The classification itself has no tunable parameters.
verb_analysis.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
result = nlp.run("verb_analysis", corpus, analysis="voice")
nlp.show(result.table, x="Document", y="Passive share", kind="bar", title="Active vs passive")

ngram_viewer.what: The familiar word-frequency-over-time chart for several phrases at once, with smoothing - a mini Ngram Viewer for your own corpus.
ngram_viewer.how: Each query's matches are counted per period and drawn as a rate series (per 1,000 words), optionally smoothed into a trend, several queries overlaid.
ngram_viewer.formula: Per-period counts divided by that period's words and scaled per 1,000. Smoothing is a moving average of window `smooth` periods (default 1 = no smoothing) - the same trick the public Ngram viewers use to quiet small-sample noise.
ngram_viewer.question: Do 'liberty' and 'equality' cross in this collection around 1900? Overlay the two series and read the crossing point, then check raw counts there.
ngram_viewer.interpretation: Rates make periods comparable; smoothing shows trend at the cost of detail (a spike of one speech disappears at smooth=5). The scale is 'per 1,000 words of this corpus', nothing larger.
ngram_viewer.limits: Rare phrases in short periods give wild rates even smoothed. Case-sensitive matching splits 'March/march'; inflections need listing (or lemma matching in scripts). This counts text, not topics - synonym series will not sum to 'the idea'.
ngram_viewer.settings: queries: your search terms (the same forms the search tool uses). case-sensitive: distinguish case. smooth: moving-average window in periods (default 1 = raw). Grouping is by the period the run form chooses.
ngram_viewer.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
series = nlp.term_rates(
    corpus,
    {"liberty": ["liberty"], "equality": ["equality"]},
    per=1000,
    by="decade",
    match="exact-lowercase",
)
nlp.show(series, x="Decade", y=["liberty per 1000", "equality per 1000"], kind="line", title="Two words over time")

sentiment_neural_bert.what: Tone per sentence and document from a small neural classifier - DistilBERT fine-tuned on movie reviews (SST-2) - the modern counterpart to VADER.
sentiment_neural_bert.how: Each sentence runs through the ONNX model (shipped with the app) and gets a positive/negative probability; documents average their sentences, with per-sentence and per-document panels.
sentiment_neural_bert.formula: DistilBERT (a distilled BERT encoder) with a classification head fine-tuned on SST-2: softmax over {negative, positive} per sentence. Document score = mean of its sentences' positive probabilities (shown also as a -1..1 rescaling of 2p-1 for comparability with VADER's compound).
sentiment_neural_bert.question: Does the neural model see the same turning points in these speeches as VADER does? Chart both and read where they diverge - the divergence is informative.
sentiment_neural_bert.interpretation: Scores are probabilities of the positive class out of the training distribution (film reviews): 0.9 is confident positive in that sense. Averaging smooths mixed documents; open the sentence view before judging one.
sentiment_neural_bert.limits: The model's world is 21st-century review English; archaic, technical or ceremonial text gets noisier. Binary sentiment only - no emotion categories, no targets/aspects. Short sentences and fragments classify shakily.
sentiment_neural_bert.settings: model: distilbert-sst2 (the shipped one). Everything else is fixed - the model file is the measurement. Scripts can also choose unit=document or sentence and pick this model through nlp.sentiment.
sentiment_neural_bert.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
tone = nlp.sentiment(corpus, model="distilbert-sst2", unit="document")
nlp.show(tone, x="Year", y="Score", kind="line", title="Neural tone over time")

sentiment_neural_spacy.what: Tone per sentence and document through spaCy's sentiment model pipeline - the same neural measurement as the BERT tool, hosted by spaCy.
sentiment_neural_spacy.how: Runs the installed spaCy model's text-classification component over each sentence and aggregates to documents; same panels as the other sentiment tools so the scores can be compared directly.
sentiment_neural_spacy.formula: spaCy's textcat component (a neural classifier) produces positive/negative probabilities per sentence; document score is the sentence mean, as in the BERT variant. Which architecture you get depends on the installed spaCy package version and model.
sentiment_neural_spacy.question: Does the choice of engine move the tone curve at all? Run it beside the BERT tool on the same corpus and compare the two lines.
sentiment_neural_spacy.interpretation: Read exactly as sentiment_neural_bert - probability of positive in the model's training sense. Differences between engines on the same text are model differences, not findings about the text.
sentiment_neural_spacy.limits: Needs the spaCy model installed (see Models). Same domain sensitivity as any review-trained classifier. Sentences are classified independently of their neighbours, so quoted irony reads straight.
sentiment_neural_spacy.settings: model: the spaCy pipeline name (en_core_web_sm is the default and what the suite installs). No other options; swap models only between runs and say so in your notes.
sentiment_neural_spacy.example:
