import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
result = nlp.run("sentiment_neural_spacy", corpus)
nlp.show(result.table, x="Document", y="Score", kind="bar", title="Tone per document")

sentiment_neural_stanza.what: Tone per sentence and document through Stanza's neural pipeline - the third engine on the same question, for triangulation.
sentiment_neural_stanza.how: Each sentence is classified by the installed Stanza sentiment model; results aggregate to documents and appear in the same panel family as the other engines.
sentiment_neural_stanza.formula: Stanza's sentiment classifier (a neural model over word and character features) scores each sentence; documents average their sentences. The scales are the model's own, so compare shapes across engines, not raw values.
sentiment_neural_stanza.question: Three engines, one corpus - do all three see the same peaks? Agreement is the finding; write up the disagreement if not.
sentiment_neural_stanza.interpretation: As the other neural tools: per-sentence probabilities averaged to documents. The panel family keeps the columns aligned so a side-by-side chart is honest.
sentiment_neural_stanza.limits: Needs the Stanza models downloaded (see Models); the first run is slow while they load. Same training-domain caveats - Stanza's sentiment data is also modern and mostly review-adjacent.
sentiment_neural_stanza.settings: language: the pipeline language ('en' default). No other options; the model package is the measurement.
sentiment_neural_stanza.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
result = nlp.run("sentiment_neural_stanza", corpus, language="en")
nlp.show(result.table, x="Document", y="Score", kind="bar", title="Tone per document")

sentiment_neural_corenlp.what: Tone per sentence and document via Stanford CoreNLP's sentiment system - the classic recursive neural sentiment model, if you run the CoreNLP server.
sentiment_neural_corenlp.how: Text is sent to a CoreNLP server you have running locally (default http://localhost:9000); its sentiment classes per sentence are collected and aggregated like the other engines'.
sentiment_neural_corenlp.formula: CoreNLP's sentiment annotator (Socher et al.'s recursive neural tensor network over parse trees): each sentence gets a 0-4 class (very negative to very positive), mapped to the common score scale in the panels. Tree-based, so it sees compositional structure the flat classifiers do not.
sentiment_neural_corenlp.question: Does the tree-structured model disagree with the flat ones on your most ambiguous texts? That is the one question this engine answers uniquely.
sentiment_neural_corenlp.interpretation: Scores are class values mapped to the shared scale - read shapes, and cross-check the panels' raw columns before quoting a number. The server's model version belongs in your notes.
sentiment_neural_corenlp.limits: Requires a separately installed and running CoreNLP server - the tool fails cleanly if it cannot reach it. Network round-trips make it the slowest of the four. The model is the oldest of the family and its training domain is movie reviews.
sentiment_neural_corenlp.settings: server: the CoreNLP URL (default http://localhost:9000). Nothing else - the annotator configuration is fixed in the suite.
sentiment_neural_corenlp.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
result = nlp.run("sentiment_neural_corenlp", corpus, server="http://localhost:9000")
nlp.show(result.table, x="Document", y="Score", kind="bar", title="Tone per document")

shape_hc.what: Story shapes by clustering: groups whole documents (or segments) into eras by their structural profile, and draws the cluster tree.
shape_hc.how: Each unit becomes a feature vector of story-shape measures, standardised per feature, then hierarchically clustered - the dendrogram is the output, and the era panel shows each cluster's shape.
shape_hc.formula: Feature standardisation first (per-feature z-scores across the units, so sentence length cannot drown everything - shape components follow units, not raw features). Then agglomerative hierarchical clustering with Ward (default), average, complete or single linkage over the standardised features; resampling (32 draws) tests how stable each split is.
shape_hc.question: Are there really three kinds of arc in this collection, or two? The dendrogram's stable splits say how many shapes there are before you name them.
shape_hc.interpretation: Clusters are groups with similar profiles under these features; the tree shows nesting (a big split into two, one of which splits again). Stability scores tell you which branches survive resampling - only those deserve names.
shape_hc.limits: Standardisation means components are relative to this corpus: add documents and old shapes shift. Linkage choice changes the tree in the middle ranks. Clusters of few units are unstable by construction.
shape_hc.settings: method: ward (default), average, complete or single - Ward for compact clusters, single for chaining effects you may want to see. n-clusters: how many groups to cut from the tree (default 2). resample: how many resampling draws for stability (default 32).
shape_hc.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
result = nlp.run("shape_hc", corpus, method="ward", n_clusters=3)
nlp.show(result.table, title="Document clusters by shape")

shape_svd.what: Story shapes by decomposition: the few latent axes along which documents' shapes vary, with each document's position on them.
shape_svd.how: Standardised shape features are reduced by SVD (the algebra behind PCA) to n components: the loadings say what each axis means, the document panel where each text sits.
shape_svd.formula: Per-feature z-scores first, then singular value decomposition of the units-by-features matrix; component 1 is the largest axis of variation in shapes (currently dominated by overall pacing/extremity), component 2 the largest remaining, and so on. Resampling (32 draws) scores how stable each component's direction is.
shape_svd.question: What is the biggest way these stories differ in shape - and does a genre or period sit at one end of it? The loadings and document positions answer in two panels.
shape_svd.interpretation: Loadings say which features make an axis (read the top positive and negative rows together). Documents at opposite ends of an axis differ along exactly those features. Explained-variance share says how much of the variety each axis holds.
shape_svd.limits: Standardised to this corpus (see shape_hc). Components beyond the first couple hold small variance and unstable directions; two runs on different corpora have different axes to compare. Sign of a component is arbitrary - read both ends.
shape_svd.settings: n-components: how many axes to keep (default 2). seed: resampling start. resample: stability draws (default 32).
shape_svd.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
result = nlp.run("shape_svd", corpus, n_components=2)
nlp.show(result.table, x="Component 1", y="Component 2", kind="scatter", title="Documents in shape space")

shape_nmf.what: Story shapes as additive parts: non-negative matrix factorisation splits shape profiles into n building blocks each document mixes in its own proportions.
shape_nmf.how: Standardised shape features are factored into parts and per-document weights - an additive reading ('this story is part steady-rise, part late-crisis') where SVD gives a subtractive axis reading.
shape_nmf.formula: Per-feature z-scores first (shifting to non-negativity for NMF), then non-negative matrix factorisation: units-by-features ~ weights x parts, fitted to minimise the Frobenius reconstruction error (Lee & Seung's multiplicative updates, up to max-iter). Parts are additive components; each document's row of weights is its composition. Resampled stability as in shape_svd.
shape_nmf.question: Which recurring building blocks of shape does this genre use, and in what proportion per story? The composition panel is the answer.
shape_nmf.interpretation: Each part is a feature profile (read its loadings); a document's weights are 'how much of each block'. Unlike SVD axes, parts can all be high at once - mixtures, not oppositions.
shape_nmf.limits: The z-score shift to non-negativity moves zero from 'average' to 'the minimum observed' - read loadings accordingly. NMF parts are not unique between runs at different seeds; stability helps but comparison across corpora stays shaky.
shape_nmf.settings: n-components: how many parts (default 2). seed: fitting and resampling start. resample: stability draws (default 32). max-iter: fitting iterations (default 200) - raise it if reconstruction error is still falling in the output.
shape_nmf.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
result = nlp.run("shape_nmf", corpus, n_components=3, seed=42)
nlp.show(result.table, kind="heatmap", title="Shape composition per document")

geocode.what: Place names in the text become coordinates: which locations these documents mention, ready for a map.
geocode.how: Locations from the named-entity tool are matched against a gazetteer (offline by default) and returned with latitude, longitude and mention counts; the map view plots them.
geocode.formula: Gazetteer lookup of each location string: exact and normalised name matching against the offline gazetteer (or the Google/ Nominatim APIs if you choose them). Counts are mentions; coordinates are the gazetteer's best entry. min-count and limit filter the result list.
geocode.question: Where do these travel writings point? Geocode them and read the map's empty regions as loudly as its clusters.
geocode.interpretation: A dot is a matched name, not a verified visit - the text mentions the place. Clusters show the corpus's geography of attention; unmatched names are the honest gap list to read by hand.
geocode.limits: Names that are also words ('Reading', 'Springfield') mis-match; translated and historical place names need the gazetteer to know them. The offline gazetteer has fixed coverage - its misses are not your documents' misses. Mentions are not locations of events.
geocode.settings: provider: offline (default, no network), google or nominatim (both send the place names to their services - use knowingly). limit: how many places to resolve (default 200). min-count: only geocode places mentioned at least this often (default 1).
geocode.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
places = nlp.run("geocode", corpus, provider="offline", min_count=2).table
nlp.show(places, x="Place", y="Count", kind="bar", title="Most mentioned places")

svo_map.what: Who does what, where: subject-verb-object triples whose place names are geocoded and mapped.
svo_map.how: Combines the SVO extraction with gazetteer coordinates - triples involving named locations become points (or arcs) on the map of the corpus's actions.
svo_map.formula: clause_svo's triple extraction (verb with nominal subject and object) plus geocode's gazetteer lookup on the triple's location mentions. Counts and rates as in the SVO tables; coordinates from the same providers as geocode.
svo_map.question: Where do the memoirs locate their actions? The mapped triples show the corpus's geography of doing rather than of mentioning.
svo_map.interpretation: Each point is a triple with a resolvable place - read the table beside the map. Shared verbs across sites are often the interesting pattern (everything 'signed' in one city).
svo_map.limits: Both parents' limits apply: missed clauses, unresolved names, ambiguous toponyms. If the SVO extraction is noisy the map is noisy - check the triples table first.
svo_map.settings: provider: offline (default), google or nominatim (names leave the machine). limit: how many places to resolve (default 200). The SVO extraction itself is fixed.
svo_map.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
result = nlp.run("svo_map", corpus, provider="offline", limit=100)
nlp.show(result.table, title="Actions by place")

word2vec_bert.what: Meaning as neighbourhoods from contextual embeddings: which words and passages stand near a query word in this corpus's usage.
word2vec_bert.how: Words (or sentences) are embedded by a small transformer, and the nearest neighbours of a query are listed - meaning as the company a word keeps here, not in a general corpus.
word2vec_bert.formula: Token embeddings from BERT-base's subword outputs (averaged per word), cosine similarity between vectors defines neighbourhoods; neighbours = highest cosine to the query vector. min-count filters hapaxes before embedding. The saved vectors are cacheable across runs (the model's work is reused when nothing changed).
word2vec_bert.question: What does 'liberty' mean in this collection specifically? Its nearest neighbours here compared with word2vec_gensim's is the whole method.
word2vec_bert.interpretation: Neighbours are the corpus's usage pattern: closer cosine = more interchangeable contexts here. The meaning-axis and meaning-group panels read semantic dimensions from the neighbour structure - treat them as descriptive, not psychological.
word2vec_bert.limits: Subword averaging mangles rare names; context is per sentence, so polysemous words blur ('bank' averages its senses). Small corpora give thin training signal - this is embedding of usage, not a trained lexical resource.
word2vec_bert.settings: field: lemma or form. model: bert-base-uncased (the shipped encoder). min-count: embed only words seen at least this often (default 2). query: the word whose neighbours you want. top-n: neighbours listed (default 5). seed: for any sampling in the panels.
word2vec_bert.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
result = nlp.run("word2vec_bert", corpus, query="liberty", top_n=10)
nlp.show(result.table, x="Neighbour", y="Cosine", kind="bar", title="Words near 'liberty'")

word2vec_gensim.what: Meaning as neighbourhoods, trained the classic way: word2vec (skip-gram or CBOW) over the corpus itself.
word2vec_gensim.how: A word2vec model is trained on the parsed text and queried for neighbours, analogy results and saved vectors - the transparent, tunable counterpart to the BERT tool.
word2vec_gensim.formula: word2vec (Mikolov et al. 2013): sg=1 trains skip-gram (predict context from word), sg=0 CBOW - over windows of `window` tokens, `vector-size` dimensions, `epochs` passes, words under min-count dropped. Neighbours by cosine; the t-SNE panel projects vectors to 2 dimensions for viewing.
word2vec_gensim.question: Does the trained-on-this-collection model place 'liberty' with political or economic company? Compare with the BERT neighbours - agreement is evidence.
word2vec_gensim.interpretation: Neighbours reflect the training corpus at these settings; window=5 catches topical rather than syntactic company. Analogy moves ('king - man + woman') are stable only on large corpora - read them as sketches.
word2vec_gensim.limits: Needs enough text to train meaningfully - tiny corpora give noise (min-count and vector-size are guards, not cures). Rare words and names are unreliable. Two runs at different seeds differ in details.
word2vec_gensim.settings: field: lemma or form. min-count: minimum occurrences to get a vector (default 2). vector-size: dimensions (default 100). window: context size in tokens (default 5). epochs: training passes (default 20). sg: 1 = skip-gram (default), 0 = CBOW. seed: training start. remove-stopwords: drop function words before training. query and top-n: which word's neighbours to show (default 5).
word2vec_gensim.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
result = nlp.run("word2vec_gensim", corpus, window=5, query="liberty", top_n=10)
nlp.show(result.table, x="Neighbour", y="Cosine", kind="bar", title="Words near 'liberty'")

lda_stability.what: Whether your topic model is real: LDA refitted at several seeds, with matched topics across runs and a stability score.
lda_stability.how: Fits the same model at every seed in the list, pairs up topics between runs by their word overlap, and reports which topics survive the refits - the honesty check before quoting any topic model.
lda_stability.formula: For each seed: gensim LDA at k topics. Topics are matched across consecutive runs by maximum Jaccard overlap of their top words; a topic is stable at stable-at (default 0.5) when its matched overlap reaches that share. The matched-topics panel shows the chains of the same topic across seeds.
lda_stability.question: Are these five themes the model found - or the seed's accident? Run five seeds and quote only the stable chains.
lda_stability.interpretation: Stable topics (long chains, high overlap) are patterns in the corpus; one-seed wonders are fitting noise. Stable-at is the bar you set for 'same topic' - 0.5 is half the top words shared.
lda_stability.limits: Overlap matching can chain-hop between similar topics; k is still imposed by you. Stability says reproducible, not true - a stable model can still be a poor description. Cost is roughly n-seeds times one LDA fit.
lda_stability.settings: topics: k per fit (default 3). seeds: comma-separated seed list (default 100,101,102). top-n: words per topic used for matching (default 10). passes: training passes per fit (default 10). stable-at: overlap share for 'same topic' (default 0.5). nouns-only: restrict vocabulary to nouns.
lda_stability.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
result = nlp.run("lda_stability", corpus, topics=3, seeds="100,101,102,103")
nlp.show(result.table, title="Topics that survive refitting")

word_sense_induction.what: The separate senses of a word in your corpus: occurrences grouped into usages, so 'bank' splits into its river and money senses here.
word_sense_induction.how: Every occurrence is embedded in its sentence context (BERT), clustered, and each cluster is a proposed sense with its example sentences - induced from the corpus, no dictionary involved.
word_sense_induction.formula: Contextual embeddings of the target word's occurrences (BERT-base over the sentence, target-token vector); k-means over those vectors into senses, sized by the split-words panel's silhouette evidence. Each sense's exemplars are the occurrences nearest its centroid.
word_sense_induction.question: How many senses of 'state' does this archive actually use? Ask for a few clusters and read the example sentences of each.
word_sense_induction.interpretation: Clusters are usage-senses in this corpus: read the exemplars before naming one. The clean-split words panel names words whose occurrences cluster most clearly - the safe cases to write about.
word_sense_induction.limits: Clusters are as many as you ask for; embeddings blur rare senses into common ones. Induced senses are corpus-relative ('the river sense here') and need not match a dictionary's divisions.
word_sense_induction.settings: field: form (default) or lemma to group occurrences. model: bert-base-uncased (the shipped encoder). The split-words and senses panels carry the cluster count and examples.
word_sense_induction.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
result = nlp.run("word_sense_induction", corpus, field="form")
nlp.show(result.table, title="Induced senses and their examples")

bert_extract.what: Extractive summary: the handful of sentences that best stand for each document, chosen by a transformer reading.
bert_extract.how: Sentences are embedded (BERT or a sentence-embedding model), and the ones most central to the document's meaning are selected in order of position - a TL;DR assembled from the text's own words.
bert_extract.formula: Sentence embeddings (mean of the model's token vectors); centrality = mean cosine of each sentence to all others in the document (or to the document's mean vector); the top `sentences` by centrality are returned in their original order.
bert_extract.question: What would a two-sentence abstract of this report be, drawn only from it? Read the extract beside the opening paragraph and compare.
bert_extract.interpretation: The extract is the document's own central sentences - a map of its focus, not a paraphrase. Central sentences are often thesis statements and repetitions; their order preserves the text's sequence.
bert_extract.limits: Extracts cannot state anything the document does not; irony and negation pass through unchanged. Centrality favours generic-but-universal sentences on short documents. The model choice moves the selection.
bert_extract.settings: sentences: how many to extract (default 3). model: bert-base-uncased (default), granite-embedding-english-r2 or qwen3-embedding-0.6b - the embedding models installed under Models; larger models give smoother centrality at a speed cost.
bert_extract.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
result = nlp.run("bert_extract", corpus, sentences=3)
nlp.show(result.table, title="Three central sentences per document")

bert_topics.what: Topics from sentence embeddings: documents (or sentences) clustered by transformer meaning, with each cluster's most typical words.
bert_topics.how: Embeds the units, clusters them into k groups, and labels each group by its highest-weight vocabulary - topics as dense regions of meaning-space rather than word co-occurrence.
bert_topics.formula: Unit embeddings from the chosen transformer (see doc_embeddings), standardised across units, then clustering into `topics` groups; cluster labels come from the most distinctive terms of the units in each cluster. The eras panel charts cluster shares over position or time.
bert_topics.question: Do these chapters form meaning-clusters the bag-of-words model missed? Compare the k=3 clustering with LDA's on the same corpus.
bert_topics.interpretation: Clusters group semantically similar units - naming one is reading its typical words and a few members. Share-over-time movement is the interesting pattern for a collection with dates.
bert_topics.limits: k is imposed; embedding models have their own blind spots (see doc_embeddings). Sentence-level runs on long corpora cost; document-level blurs mixed documents into one vector. Two models need not find the same clusters.
bert_topics.settings: topics: number of clusters (default 3). top-n: typical words listed per topic (default 5). seed: clustering start (default 42). model: bert-base-uncased (default), granite-embedding-english-r2 or qwen3-embedding-0.6b.
bert_topics.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
result = nlp.run("bert_topics", corpus, topics=3, seed=42)
nlp.show(result.table, title="Meaning clusters")

doc_embeddings.what: Documents as points in meaning-space: similarity, neighbours and a map by transformer embeddings, plus search-by-meaning across the corpus.
doc_embeddings.how: Every document (or sentence) is embedded by a small transformer; outputs are a similarity heat map, each unit's nearest neighbours, a 2-D map and a search panel answering 'what is closest to this sentence'.
doc_embeddings.formula: Embeddings from the chosen model (mean-pooled token vectors over the unit; sentence or document unit). Similarity = cosine between vectors, shown as the heat map and neighbour lists. The map panel projects with t-SNE; search_results ranks units by cosine to the query's embedding. Vectors are cached across runs keyed by model, model file and item texts - a second run over unchanged documents recomputes nothing.
doc_embeddings.question: What in this archive is closest in meaning to 'a promise of freedom'? Search-by-meaning finds passages TF-IDF synonyms would miss.
doc_embeddings.interpretation: Cosine near 1 means near-interchangeable contexts to the model, not agreement or quotation. The map's geometry is a projection - distances between far clusters are less meaningful than within them.
doc_embeddings.limits: Transformers blur nuance and carry their training biases; negation and irony get flattened. Unit choice matters: a mixed document's mean vector is a compromise. t-SNE maps are non-deterministic between runs at the details level.
doc_embeddings.settings: model: bert-base-uncased, granite-embedding-english-r2 (default) or qwen3-embedding-0.6b. unit: document (default) or sentence. top-n: neighbours listed (default 5). query: the sentence or phrase to search by meaning. seed: projection/clustering start (default 42).
doc_embeddings.example:
import nlpsuite as nlp

corpus = nlp.corpus()
result = nlp.similar(corpus, "a promise of freedom", unit="sentence")
nlp.show(result, x="Document", y="Similarity", kind="bar", title="Passages closest to the query")
